title: Working With Upset
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva as a source of practical help for working with anger, fear, and despair, offered at Samish as the "how" to follow Tim's talk on why we practice. Kanho tells how Shantideva, according to the stories, answered a hostile Nalanda assembly with a teaching so deep that his seat rose into the sky. Verses on the rope of mindfulness tethering the elephant of the mind, on wrapping leather around the feet instead of covering the earth, and on a single flash of anger shattering a thousand ages of good works anchor suggestions to feel the body, work on the mind rather than the world, and remember anger as the enemy. The last suggestion, dis-identification, means stepping back from conditioned thinking, such as Kanho's own habit of working harder when going the wrong way.

sentences.text: The three, and then everybody would say good, bad, or so-so, but I think I'm going to borrow Cathy Fischer's method.
Why don't you give me a thumbs up, a thumbs down, or a sideways on the count of three.
One, two, three.
Looks like we're doing pretty good.
So I want to tell you this is my first ever dharma talk at Samish, and I'm not nervous at all.
I did not jump the gun and run in early.
I did not put on my okesa inside out over my t-shirt and pants.
All these things did not happen.
But before I start with the talk, I want to thank Norman and Tim for inviting me to do this.
I'm so moved and grateful for their continued support.
I have been coming here for 17 or 18 years, and looking around, I see changes in the grounds and the buildings.
Some are looking better.
Some are a little bit more worn, like me.
But what strikes me most is the timeless feeling of the landscape, the water, the islands.
A couple of days ago, I saw a man rowing a small boat towards the shore in that golden orange light of the setting sun, the water still and reflective, which is pretty rare around here.
He came from working the oyster beds, I would guess.
The image in my mind was standing for all the years.
The sea has provided food for those living on her shores.
I love being here on Samish Island, and I am so happy that the Red Cedar Zen community continues to make it possible.
I appreciated Tim's talk yesterday.
It is good to be reminded why we are here at sesshin, sitting together.
We have so many options for what to do with our lives, and yet here we are, looking at the wall and investigating the mind.
And when we are about to fall into another trap of our own making, we should run the koan dialogues through our mind.
"Be aware."
"Yes, yes."
"Don't be deceived."
"No, no."
So Tim gave us the why for our practice.
That was really good.
It felt like a balance held up by Zazen and aspiration.
Then I wondered if I could maybe offer some support about the how while we are here and when we are back home.
Maybe you would like to try on one or another of the suggestions.
If not, please just sit and don't let my words disturb your Zazen.
So much goes on that does not support meditation.
Anger, sleepiness, sleeplessness, daydreaming, raw emotion, regrets, blaming, fear, they all show up in random order to unsettle us.
Samish is a safe place, and while we are here, the world goes on.
Politics, global warming, families separated and kids held in cages.
Corruption, lies, fear.
I could continue.
And sooner or later, we will return to the world of 24-hour news, Internet, lots of talking, and our news bubble.
We are surrounded by it.
Can we avoid the traps?
Probably not completely.
However, I would like to offer some practices that have really supported me at times.
The question is, how can we hold all this beauty and all the concern at the same time?
What can help us at sesshin?
What can we use right here?
What can we use at home?
What can we do when thoughts keep on coming that lead towards anger and despair?
When I push my own buttons to go down that familiar path.
What is difficult or painful cannot be pushed away.
Suppressing our problems will only temporarily make them hide until they burst out in some unexpected place in a new form.
In one of his talks several years ago, Norman spoke of never turning away.
And that phrase was a game changer for me.
Not that it was the first time I've heard it, but I heard it on a different level.
Never turning away from what is painful, difficult, scary.
Staying with unease without aggression and blame.
Staying with it until I get to know it as much as I can.
I do that a lot during sesshin.
And I'm almost sure I'm not the only one.
To prepare this talk, I used Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva, one of my favorite Dharma books.
I used it for guidance and also to provide some eloquence.
I need all the help I can get.
Oh, and Shantideva talks much about fools and unlearned worldlings.
And I recognize myself in that all the time.
Shantideva probably had some sense of humor too.
Here is a bit more about Shantideva himself.
He was born a prince in 8th century India.
However, the night before he was to take the throne, he left.
There are different stories why he decided not to take the power and prestige that was promised.
He came to Nalanda, the big Buddhist university, and it seems that he did not make many friends there.
The other students wanted to get rid of him and they hoped that embarrassment would do it.
They asked him to give a teaching.
And they thought that this guy whose main practices seemed to be sleeping, eating, and, the literature says, shitting, would truly fail.
But his response was the Way of the Bodhisattva.
He was so eloquent and so deep that when he spoke about wisdom his seat rose higher and higher until he himself disappeared in the white sky while his voice penetrated all the way to the assembly.
That was, by the way, the last they ever saw of him.
So I did turn to the Way of the Bodhisattva for help.
How to tackle difficult patterns that exist in us and around us.
The first set is from the chapter on diligent introspection.
My mind is like a kid in the candy store.
It gets distracted and there are so many toys with my name on them.
The scattered mind is easily distracted, and emotions inside and the world outside will keep it happily entertained and distracted.
The standard lures of greed, hate, and delusion do cause much happiness, unhappiness.
The first step, Shantideva says, is to tame the mind with the rope of mindfulness.
Mindfulness brings the mind back to the present.
This breath, this step, this moment, pleasant or unpleasant is not the question.
The question is: what is this?
What is real?
So I said Shantideva would provide eloquence.
Here he goes.
*If with mindfulness's rope the elephant of the mind is tethered all around, our fears will come to nothing.
Every virtue drops into our hands.
Tigers, lions, elephants, and bears, snakes, and every hostile foe.
Those who guard the prisoners in hell.
All ghosts and every evil phantom.
By simple binding of this mind alone all these things are likewise bound.
By simple binding of this mind alone all these things are likewise bound.*
This is so hard and so easy at the same time.
I'm being very mindful and settled and all of a sudden I realize that I dream of having a horse, that I was vacationing in Bali, and so on.
The good news is that recognizing the fact that I got sidetracked is a moment of mindfulness and I can return to my practice.
I do know that this random wishing and dreaming does not lead to happiness.
Shantideva is much harsher.
He calls it honey on the razor's edge.
So here's suggestion number one.
Focusing on the body, feeling the gravity holding us on the chair or the cushion, becoming keenly aware of all physical sensation.
Contact with the floor, the chair, clothing, temperature.
If you cannot connect with this, maybe do a body scan to pull you back into your body in this moment.
So suggestion number two is Shantideva giving us an idea how to deal with obstacles that arise in front of us, like a sharp stone or an uneven road.
He says:
*To cover all the earth with sheets of hide, the sheets of hide.
Where could such amounts of skin be found?
But simply wrap some leather around your feet and it's as if the whole world had been covered.
Likewise, we can never take and turn aside the outer course of things but only seize and discipline the mind itself.
What is there remaining to be curbed?*
So we've probably all found out that we're not masters of this universe.
We cannot snap our fingers and the world will change to our liking.
And what would we do if the person next to us snapped their finger and wished the opposite?
So when we see the rough ground with sharp rocks, we have a choice.
We can demand that someone paves over all the unpleasantness.
Good luck with that.
Or we can put on some sturdy hiking boots and start exploring.
Oh yes, I make mistakes all the time.
I go the wrong way until I figure things out a bit better.
I trip a few times.
But I also will figure out how to cross that territory.
Those sharp rocks are not the fault of the evil world.
They simply exist.
And just like we fortify our feet with boots, we can fortify our mind to protect it from injury.
And we can do that with mindfulness.
When we live in our body in real time, our head has much less of an opportunity to run us in circles, to tell us that blaming someone or assigning fault is surely the right thing.
And it sounds unsophisticated, but his suggestion is actually what works.
I cannot change the world, a little bit maybe, but I need to do the work on myself.
There I do have a lot of influence.
The next suggestions I took from the chapter on patience.
It is interesting that the chapter is titled patience, but the word patience hardly ever appears.
But there is much talk about anger.
Shantideva describes the harm it does to us, and I found that out for myself.
When I am sitting and anger arises, I notice the muscle tension, the desire to move, to do something.
The breath comes a little faster.
The nervous tension increases.
Nowadays, I know that this anger stress response affects body and mind in many ways.
Down on the ground level, I would say that anger almost always makes me do unwise things or say unwise things.

I have learned intellectually that this repeated fear and anger pattern will predispose my mind to use anger as a default and that triggering the anger will become easier and easier as time passes by.
So when anger takes hold of me, I remember this.
Do I want to give away the power I have, the power over my actions, over my feelings?
Is this the way that, when external events and internal emotions occur, I give up on my practice and let these waves that come and go push me around?
Sometimes it truly helps to think my way through anger, and with repeated practice, it has become easier.
So Shantideva has much to say about anger, what it does and how to work with it.
I wish I could just sit here and read the whole chapter to you and then follow it up with Norman's chapter on patience, on the perfection of patience, in his new book, The World Could Be Otherwise.
I can't, so I will cherry pick a bit of Shantideva.
He gives us a very gentle introduction.
*Good works gathered in a thousand ages, such as deeds of generosity or offerings of the blissful ones, a single flash of anger shatters them.*
I know it sounds exaggerated, but a long, long time relationship can be destroyed by one flash of anger, and often we can repair it, but there is a knot in that rope that will always remain.
*Those tormented by the pain of anger will never know tranquility of mind.
Strangers they will be to every pleasure.
Sleep departs them.
They can never rest.
Getting what I don't want and all that hinders my desire, there my mind feels fueled for misery.
Anger springs from it, oppressing me.*
So he writes about the danger being anger itself.
The person acting out on anger is not our enemy.
It is the anger itself, and it is difficult to hold that in mind when the feelings are running high.
I think his antidote to it is sweet.
He recognizes that anger does occur.
We need to deal with it and let it harm us.
*So come what may, I'll never harm my cheerful happiness of mind.
Depression never brings me what I want.
My virtue will be warped and marred by it.*
And when I read that the first time, I saw the other truth of the statement for me, and it has become much harder to escape the self-indulgence of discouragement and depression.
And when my mind goes to Shantideva, he unwinds my story line, my blame story most of the time.
It was so and so and this and that.
Insert the appropriate phrase of the day.
He encourages us to endure, to follow our practice and to return to the current moment, and especially to refrain from retaliation.
And he explains a little more what this anger looks like on the other side, from the perspective of the person who is angry.
*Never thinking, "Now I will be angry," people impulsively are caught up in anger.
Irritation likewise comes though never planned to be experienced.
Conditions once assembled have no thought that now they will rise to some result, and that which is engendered does not think that it has been produced by such conditions.*
He really asked for compassion with the angry person.
Practicing this over time will lead to a greater understanding of anger when we encounter it, and maybe we ourselves can also be moved to compassion.
While anger does give a burst of energy, we do know that it makes a sad life and that it warps our relationships.
Our companions have little choice.
They can either match our anger with their own or they can submit to our outbursts, and we should think about that.
Maybe they are wise in the use of patience, but let's not test them like this.
I encourage you to sit with what Shantideva says about causes and conditions triggering anger and how helpless us humans are in its grip, and the worst thing is we feel so righteous and justified.
One more Shantideva quote.
Remember when I said that he had a sense of humor?
Sometimes he seems to really agree with us and then he turns it around 180 degrees.
So after praising our practice of patience, he adds a little zinger to shift our perspective.
*Because of them and through my patience all my sins are cleansed and purified, but they, the ones who have anger, they will be the ones who thanks to me will have the long drawn out agonies of hell.
Therefore I am their tormentor.
Therefore it is they who bring me benefit.
Thus with what perversity, pernicious mind, will you be angry with your enemies?*
So I just really like that.
The way he twists my smugness and righteousness.
Oh, I've been so patient with this person.
They're so bad.
I just think this is very fine.
I would love to meet Shantideva and sit down and talk with him.
In a way I do, though it feels like a very one-sided conversation.
Most of the time at least.
And thank you for indulging me, letting me talk about one of my favorite books.
I have come a long way and I do have a long way to go.
Shantideva has been a really steady companion.
So my last suggestion has one foot in Zen practice and the other in mindfulness practice.
It is called dis-identification.
You probably have heard that old joke: I finally gave up smoking and now they call me a quitter.
How often have you had the experience that you do something that feels really right and good, but you drop it because you talk yourself out of it?
We always find reasons not to pursue things.
Not enough time, not enough energy, not this, not that.
So we stop, and the same thoughts that talk you into quitting now beat you up for it.
Having thoughts and habits following the thoughts can be a pattern in our life.
We may want to be watchful and see what is happening.
We notice that our thoughts are not consistent.
They can flip on short notice from enthusiasm to aversion.
I guess that's where the saying comes from that you should not always believe your thoughts.
No matter how much we can make ourselves fall in love with them.
The tool of dis-identification means to intentionally take one step back and watch our conditioned mind doing its routine without getting caught up in it.
The latest drama, the juiciest thought, the best blaming pattern.
Without getting caught up in all the self-judgment that comes with it, let us not be limited by conditioned thinking.
The process we use as a default, whatever content may be, let us be careful about these habits.
While they can serve us very well in some conditions, they also absolutely rule us when we are on autopilot.
If we use the same process for just about everything, without being careful, it can lead to great misunderstanding.
I myself, well, my conditioning from early on, my process was to work harder and longer when I failed at something.
And yes, it did serve me at times, but I also used the same process when I was going in the wrong direction.
Well, you can push back as hard as you want if you're going the wrong way, it's not helpful.
And that's what I did quite a lot, and that's what I still do.
So do you see how that can be a problem?
If you're trailblazing, just make sure that it's not your old habits.
Yes, even when we carefully investigate where we go, we still will go down the wrong alley.
But when we're disidentified, we're not so much in love with the direction we chose, we're more open to input.
So that thought about carefully looking at what we're doing leads us back to diligent introspection and to the end of my talk.
If you found something useful in this talk, you may consider trying it out and trying it on for a while.
If there is nothing useful in this talk, please forget every word I said.
Thank you very much.
*Don't be deceived.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
